slides.title: Classification of acid–base disturbances and compensation
bullets: Acidosis is an absolute or relative increase in H⁺ with a fall in pH; alkalosis is an absolute or relative decrease in H⁺ with a rise in pH.

pH depends not on the absolute amounts of bicarbonate and carbonic acid but on their ratio; a primary change in bicarbonate leads to a metabolic disturbance, a primary change in carbonic acid to a respiratory one.

A respiratory (gas) disturbance is impaired CO₂ elimination in respiratory failure (acidosis) or lung hyperventilation (alkalosis); a metabolic (non-gas) one is a gain or loss of acids or bases due to disturbed metabolism, excretion or exogenous intake.

Causes of metabolic acidosis: metabolic disturbances (hypoxia, diabetic coma), impaired excretion (renal failure, prolonged diarrhoea), exogenous intake (food, drugs) and mixed causes (for example shock).

slides.title: Classification of acid–base disturbances and compensation
bullets: Causes of metabolic alkalosis: large loss of acids (repeated vomiting) or intake of a large amount of basic substances.
A primary respiratory change is compensated by a metabolic one, and a primary metabolic change by a change in breathing (for example, in metabolic acidosis hyperventilation lowers CO₂).

slides.title: Respiratory acidosis
bullets: Causes: injury, inflammation or drug-induced depression of the respiratory centre; weak respiratory muscles; reduced respiratory surface of the lungs (pneumonia, atelectasis, tumours, emphysema, pneumothorax); impaired airway patency or aspiration of foreign material; status asthmaticus; spasm of the vocal cords.
In uncompensated acidosis the CO₂ pressure rises and pH falls; there is no metabolic compensation, so the alkaline reserve is unchanged (BE, BB, AB, SB normal).

If it is compensated by metabolic changes, buffer bases rise (BE shifts to the positive side, BB and AB above normal) and despite the excess CO₂ pH approaches or reaches normal — respiratory acidosis compensated by metabolic alkalosis.

slides.title: Respiratory acidosis
bullets: Buffer systems join the compensation first, then the kidneys: H⁺ is actively secreted in the tubules, titratable acids and ammonium chloride are excreted in the urine (acid urine reaction) and bicarbonate reabsorption speeds up; proteins bind H⁺.
Metabolic compensation cannot fully offset impaired lung function; it is effective in moderate ventilation disturbances and chronic hypercapnia.

Hypercapnia dilates cerebral vessels and raises intracranial pressure, constricts peripheral arterioles and raises blood pressure, and lowers haemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen; if compensation is insufficient, metabolic acidosis may be added.

slides.title: Metabolic acidosis
bullets: Metabolic acidosis is the most severe and the most common acid–base disturbance.

Causes: any hypoxia (exogenous, circulatory, respiratory, haemic, tissue), diabetes mellitus, starvation, fever, renal failure, prolonged diarrhoea, widespread inflammatory processes (peritonitis), excessive intake of calcium chloride or ammonium chloride.
When uncompensated, blood pH falls because bases fall (BE shifts to the negative side; AB, BB, SB below normal), while pCO₂ is unchanged.

If it is compensated by lung hyperventilation, pCO₂ falls (hypocapnia) and despite the low bicarbonate pH approaches normal — metabolic acidosis compensated by respiratory alkalosis; the typical sign is Kussmaul’s deep, noisy breathing.

slides.title: Metabolic acidosis
bullets: The kidneys (acido- and ammoniogenesis) and liver join the compensation; because H⁺ pushes K⁺ out of cells, plasma potassium rises; when diabetic coma is treated with insulin, hyperkalaemia can quickly switch to hypokalaemia as K⁺ starts entering cells.
Clinical signs differ little from respiratory acidosis, so a correct assessment requires the objective acid–base indices and the pathogenesis of the underlying disease.

slides.title: The role of the kidneys in maintaining acid–base balance
bullets: The kidneys have a marked effect on acid–base balance, but it shows later than the action of the lungs: the lungs begin to normalise the H⁺ concentration within minutes, the kidneys act much more slowly.
The main mechanism is sodium reabsorption and hydrogen-ion secretion in the cells of the renal tubules; it works through three chemical processes.

1) Sodium reabsorption with conversion of monohydrogen phosphate to dihydrogen phosphate: in blood the dihydrogen-to-monohydrogen phosphate ratio is about 1:4; as the tubular fluid is acidified the dihydrogen form comes to predominate and is excreted in the urine.

2) Conversion of bicarbonate to carbonic acid in the tubule lumen: in tubular cells carbonic anhydrase makes carbonic acid from CO₂ and water, its H⁺ goes into the lumen; bicarbonate is formed and the alkaline reserve of the blood is restored.

slides.title: The role of the kidneys in maintaining acid–base balance
bullets: 3) Ammonia formation in the kidney: from the breakdown of glutamine by the enzyme glutaminase (highest activity in kidney tissue); ammonia is used to neutralise and excrete acids in place of other cations.
The urine-to-blood H⁺ concentration ratio can reach 800:1, showing the high ability of the kidney to excrete hydrogen ions.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. Sodium is the main extracellular cation (normal ~136–145 mmol/L), determines osmolality and volume; potassium is the main intracellular cation (~3.5–5.0 mmol/L), membrane potential, heart rhythm; chloride is the main anion, acid-base balance.

2. Method – ion-selective electrodes (ISE): direct (undiluted – blood gas analyzers) and indirect (diluted – large biochemistry analyzers); with indirect ISE, hyperlipidemia and hyperproteinemia give false hyponatremia.

3. Potassium preanalytics: hemolysis, fist clenching, prolonged tourniquet, K-EDTA contamination, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis (in serum) give false hyperkalemia – when in doubt remeasure in heparinized plasma; storage in the cold also raises K.
4. Hyponatremia: water excess (SIADH, heart/liver failure), Na loss (diuretics, vomiting, adrenal insufficiency); hypernatremia – water loss, diabetes insipidus.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 5. Hyperkalemia: renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, drugs, cell breakdown, acidosis; hypokalemia: diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, hyperaldosteronism, alkalosis.
6. Chloride: falls in metabolic alkalosis (vomiting), rises in hyperchloremic acidosis; used in interpreting the anion gap (Na − (Cl + HCO3)).

slides.title: Biological significance of water-electrolyte metabolism?
bullets: 1. Water makes up ~60% of body weight in adults: ~2/3 inside cells, ~1/3 outside cells (interstitial and intravascular).
2. Water is a solvent and transport medium, thermoregulation, the medium of metabolic reactions.

3. Electrolytes: Na⁺ – the main cation of extracellular fluid (osmolality and volume), K⁺ – intracellular (membrane potential, neuromuscular excitability), Cl⁻ and HCO3⁻ – the main anions (acid-base balance), Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ – enzymes, contraction, hemostasis.
4. Plasma osmolality (~275–295 mOsm/kg) is determined mainly by Na; oncotic pressure is provided by albumin.
5. Disorders: dehydration/overhydration, imbalance of sodium and potassium – neurological and cardiac complications; laboratory monitoring – electrolytes, osmolality, hematocrit, protein.

slides.title: Regulation of water-electrolyte metabolism?
bullets: 1. Osmoregulation: hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense a rise in plasma osmolality → thirst and secretion of ADH (vasopressin) → via V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts aquaporin-2 – water reabsorption.
2. Volume regulation: the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system – aldosterone in the distal nephron increases Na reabsorption and K excretion; its secretion is regulated by K⁺ level and the RAAS.
3. Natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) – natriuresis and vasodilation when volume increases.
4. The kidney is the final effector organ: filtration, reabsorption, concentration.
5. Laboratory reflection: plasma and urine osmolality, Na, K, urine Na; ADH disorders – diabetes insipidus (urine dilute, hypernatremia), SIADH (hyponatremia, urine concentrated).
